# develop-cycle

**[Flow map](FLOW.md)** shows every agent, gate, loop and terminal state, generated by running the engine.

develop is the build workflow. It builds the `todo` blocks of one approved plan file in a worktree of
your repo and keeps each block once it passes review. When the plan is done, the accepted work lands on
the branch you have checked out, staged for you to commit or committed for you.

Each `## Plan:` block names its `mode`, and the mode picks the instructions the engine gives its agents.

| Mode | One block is | Acceptance checks |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| `feature` | One bounded feature, such as a new endpoint, MCP tool, page or form | The criteria are met and the feature is wired in and reachable |
| `section` | One slice of a goal that spans many call sites, such as a migration or upgrade | The criteria are met and every call site the block owns is converted |
| `fix` | One triaged issue inventory from debug or your own testing | Each ACTIONABLE issue is fixed at its root cause and no other entry was touched |

A block can also name its developer model in a `model:` line (`opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku` or `fable`), picked
by the task. Sonnet takes common work, opus takes complex or risky work, haiku takes a bulk text
replacement, and fable runs only when you ask for it. The review roles use the run's `models`, which
default to Opus, and every role runs at the `high` reasoning level unless the run's `efforts` says
otherwise. A block's `effort:` line (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`) sets its developer's level
instead, and Claude writes one only when you ask for a level other than the run's. Claude saves the role
models and efforts you ask to keep for a repo in the repo's project settings with `project-settings.mjs
set-roles`, and the next run of that repo takes them from `project-settings.mjs roles`. A role you name for a run wins
over the saved one.

The first run in a repo asks every setup question in one prompt and saves the answers, so later runs
ask nothing. A run's `changePolicy` is `focused` by default. The saved policy is `focused`, `proactive`
or `auto`. With `auto`, Claude picks `focused` or
`proactive` for each run and shows the reason in the approval summary. The developer sorts the code into
three zones. Task code is the code its block changes. In a fix block, it also holds every repeat of the
problem each entry names. Connected code is the code that calls or repeats task code, and the docs that
describe it. Code another block of the plan owns is never task or connected code. Other code is everything
else.

Under both policies, the developer fixes every problem in task code at any size. It also fixes a
problem its change causes or exposes in connected code. It never changes other code. When its change
causes or exposes a problem there, it fixes the cause in task or connected code. If only a change in
other code can fix the problem, the developer escalates it. `focused` is for working code that stays
close to the task. Its developer builds minimally. It leaves unchanged any problem the connected code
already had that its change neither causes nor exposes. `proactive` is for the best code. Its developer
builds each feature and section block with the change that has the best long-term result. In those
blocks, it also fixes a defect the connected code already had when the fix is low risk. It records a
cleanup outside task code, such as a clearer name, in the backlog and leaves the code unchanged. A
`proactive` run also builds every ready entry in the project's backlog before it lands, so it fixes issues
across the codebase over time. It uses more tokens per run, and fewer in total than reaching the same code
quality later. A `focused` run builds the backlog only when you ask.

The delivery setting picks how the work lands. With `stage`, the run's entire change lands staged in your
checkout, so you review it and commit. With `commit`, each accepted block that changed code is one commit
whose message is the block's title, and your branch moves to those commits when the run lands. Your
repo's commit hooks run, and a commit that a hook or signing refuses halts the run with the block's work
staged.

The run builds in a worktree beside your repo, so you can keep working in your checkout. When your
branch gained commits during the run, the run is rebased onto them and its gate runs again before it
lands. Claude resolves a conflict itself and names each file it resolved. Your uncommitted work stays
where it is, and Claude asks you only when it sits at a path the run changed.

## How it works

Every block runs the same loop, up to `maxRounds`.

1. A **developer** works in six phases and leaves its work unstaged.
   - **Patterns.** It finds how the repo already does the same kind of thing.
   - **Build.** It builds the block and runs the gates. In a round that answers a review, it fixes or
     logs each finding in that review. A feature or section block does not build the block again in
     that round, and a fix block still works through its entries. Each later phase runs only a
     targeted test of its changes. The gates run once more after the last phase that changed code, and
     a phase with nothing to do is skipped.
   - **Harden.** It handles edge cases, gives each expected failure a message that names its cause and
     adds a test for each risky path. It also cleans up the code its round wrote.
   - **Siblings.** It fixes every repeat of a problem it fixed inside the code its policy lets it
     change, and logs the rest.
   - **Self-review.** It applies the blind reviewer's checks to the code its round changed or read.
     Each earlier round had its own self-review, and each blind review checks the entire block. So the
     self-review skips code that earlier rounds changed unless this round changed or read it.
   - **Classify.** It judges the risk of each change its round made with four questions. A change is
     low risk when it needs edits in only one system, adds few branches or error paths, touches no
     critical code such as data writes or security, and rests on no assumption a caller could break.
     A doubtful answer counts as risky. It also records a snapshot of its round's tree, so acceptance
     can read that round's own changes.
2. A **blind quality reviewer** judges the unstaged diff on its own merits. It never sees the plan.
   Under both policies, it reports every problem it finds, from critical down to nit. It reviews the
   block's first round that meets its gate, and any later round with a change the developer judged
   risky. A round with only low-risk changes goes straight to acceptance.
3. An **acceptance verifier** checks the diff against the block and stages it on a pass. In commit
   mode it also commits it.
   It also rechecks every finding raised earlier in the block. For a round the blind reviewer did not
   see, it checks each of the developer's risk answers against that round's own changes. A wrong answer
   sends the next round to the blind reviewer.
4. If the last round fails, a **closing pass** runs one more developer, and no develop round follows
   it. It makes each fix that is low risk and records each risky fix in the project's backlog. A blind
   review follows it when its changes need one. Then acceptance runs once more and sorts each problem
   it finds as blocking or not blocking. A regression, a failing gate, an unmet requirement and a
   serious defect the block adds are blocking. With no blocking problem, acceptance lands the block
   and records each other problem in the backlog.
5. A block that cannot pass is **parked**. Its work is saved as a commit on a branch and cleared from
   the tree, so nothing is lost and the next block starts clean. One entry in the project's backlog
   links the branch and says why the block parked. Once that entry is ready to build, a later fix run
   restores the branch's work and finishes it.

Settings at the top of the plan file control the run.

- `ordered: true` stops the run at a parked block, since later blocks depend on it.
- `suite: scoped` lets the existing test suite stay red mid-run, as a test-first migration expects.
- `sweep: goal-coverage` runs a final check of the `goal:` line across the entire repo once every block
  is done.

A file with a `section` block defaults to `ordered: true`, `suite: scoped` and `sweep: goal-coverage`.

## How to use it

Install the `aipg` plugin, or clone the repo as `aipg/` and drive it by path.

- **Skill:** `/aipg:develop add a search_docs MCP tool. Plan it first.`
- **Plain pointer:** tell Claude to use the develop workflow in `aipg/workflows/develop/`.

Claude reads `workflows/develop/CLAUDE.md` and follows it.

1. Claude writes the plan file with you in plan mode.
2. The [refine](../refine/) workflow reviews the plan until it has no defects left.
3. You approve the final plan text.
4. develop builds the blocks.
5. Before each launch, `tools/plan-edit.mjs args` writes the results of every finished run into the
   plan file's `status:` lines. A relaunch then builds only what is still `todo`.

For a debug inventory, triage the issue files first. Each one is a fix-mode plan file develop builds
directly.

## Reviewing the result

Run the tests yourself and read `git diff --cached`. The run folder `runs/<runId>/` holds the
acceptance reviews, the quality reviews under `gate/`, the developer's risk answers for each round
(`risk-<id>-rN.md`, which starts with the round's snapshot), each block's declined findings
(`gate/DISMISSED-<id>.md`), any plan amendment
(`AMENDED-<id>.md`), the questions that stopped an ordered run (`NEEDS-USER.md`), an unordered
run's question for one block (`question-<id>.md`, which the park also copies into that block's backlog
entry), the
defaults the developer took, a pointer to each plan amendment and each fix the developer made to a
problem the code already had that its block did not require (`DECISIONS.md`), and the sweep result
(`SWEEP.md`).

The project's backlog folder (`backlog/<project>/`) holds the defects found outside each block's work,
in one file per block of each run. From a block's closing pass, it holds the findings whose fixes need
a blind review and each problem that acceptance did not count as blocking. Under `proactive`, it also
holds the cleanups the developer noticed and did not make. Under both policies, it holds each
feature or refactor the developer noticed outside a block's scope, each choice it escalated and
proceeded past by a default, and one entry per parked block. Each entry says whether it is ready to
build. An entry is `ACTIONABLE` when it is a defect or a cleanup with one clear, small fix that
changes no user-visible behavior, stored data or public contract. Develop builds it without triage.
Every other entry is `NEEDS_USER` and waits for you. To work the backlog, run
`/aipg:develop work the backlog`, or tell Claude to work the backlog with the develop workflow. You
triage the `NEEDS_USER` entries with Claude. Then develop builds the `ACTIONABLE` entries and the
entries you approve.

## Requirements

- **Claude Code** with the background **Workflow** capability.
- A target git repo, plus a build command and a test command.
